paragraphs.heading: The question at the heart of RSA
paragraphs.text: The RSA problem is the task of carrying out a private-key operation using nothing but the public key. RSA works by raising a message to a power, called the exponent, modulo a composite number N, and nobody else knows the factors of N. Seen that way, breaking it means finding e-th roots of an arbitrary number modulo N.

paragraphs.heading: Stating it precisely
paragraphs.text: Written out exactly, the public key is the pair (N, e), and the ciphertext is C ≡ Pᵉ (mod N); the task is to find the original message P quickly. N must be a large semiprime, meaning a product of two large prime numbers. The exponent must satisfy 2 < e < N and be coprime to φ(N), and the ciphertext must satisfy 0 ≤ C < N. C is picked at random from that range, and a fully precise statement also depends on how N and e were generated.

paragraphs.heading: Why the problem matters
paragraphs.text: For large RSA keys, over 1024 bits, nobody knows an efficient way to solve this problem. If someone found one, it would put RSA-based systems at risk, both for encrypting messages and for digital signatures. Yet there is no proof that the problem is hard, just as there is no proof that factoring whole numbers is hard.

paragraphs.heading: The factoring route
paragraphs.text: The best known attack is to factor the modulus N first, a task thought to be impractical when N is big enough. Once the prime factors are known, the same steps RSA uses during key setup turn the public exponent e into the private exponent d. So anyone who factors N gets the private key, and with it can decrypt any ciphertext.

paragraphs.heading: Maybe easier than factoring
paragraphs.text: That attack shows the RSA problem is no harder than factoring, but it could be easier. There is strong evidence that a way to break RSA would not necessarily give a way to factor large semiprimes. Factoring is overkill: the RSA problem only asks to decrypt one ciphertext, while factoring hands over the private key, which opens every ciphertext and allowing any private-key operation. Finding the private exponent d, though, is just as hard as factoring N, even though the RSA problem never asks for d.

paragraphs.heading: Padding closes a side door
paragraphs.text: RSA also has a particular mathematical structure that an attacker might exploit without solving the RSA problem at all. To get the full strength the problem promises, a system built on RSA must also use a padding scheme such as OAEP, which guards against these structural weaknesses.
